cv_interview_alignment.summary: The biggest gap is between the CV's portrayal of a full-stack, cloud-native engineer with deep infrastructure expertise and the interview reality of a frontend-focused developer who defers on backend, DevOps, and ML topics. The market for FAANG grad roles expects candidates to own end-to-end features and demonstrate hands-on experience with the technologies on their CV.

gap_analysis.market_context: FAANG and top-tier companies value candidates who can demonstrate ownership of complex, cross-functional features. For grad roles, they look for evidence of hands-on coding, problem-solving, and the ability to learn and apply new technologies independently. Marcus's CV suggests he has this, but the interview reveals a reliance on teammates for the hard parts.

project_suggestions.title: Deploy a personal project end-to-end with Docker, Kubernetes, and CI/CD
project_suggestions.why: Addresses the gap between claiming Kubernetes/Docker experience and actually owning the deployment. A simple web app deployed on a cloud provider with a full CI/CD pipeline will demonstrate hands-on infrastructure skills.
project_suggestions.outcome: In your next interview, you can say: 'I containerized my app with Docker, set up a Kubernetes cluster on AWS, and automated deployments with GitHub Actions. I handled service discovery, rolling updates, and monitoring.'

project_suggestions.title: Build a real-time data pipeline with Kafka and Redis
project_suggestions.why: Directly addresses the gap in Kafka and Redis knowledge claimed on the CV. A simple streaming app (e.g., Twitter sentiment analysis) will force hands-on experience with Kafka producers/consumers and Redis data structures.
project_suggestions.outcome: You can say: 'I built a real-time data pipeline using Kafka for ingestion and Redis for in-memory aggregation. I managed consumer groups, handled partitioning, and used Redis Sorted Sets for real-time leaderboards.'

project_suggestions.title: Contribute to an open-source project's frontend performance
project_suggestions.why: Leverages Marcus's existing frontend strength while building credibility in a visible, collaborative environment. Choose a project with complex data visualizations (e.g., Apache Superset, Grafana) to showcase D3.js and performance optimization skills.
project_suggestions.outcome: You can say: 'I contributed performance optimizations to an open-source dashboard project, reducing re-render flicker by implementing virtual DOM diffing — a technique I first explored on a personal project.'

interview_tips.observation: When asked about StockSense performance, you said 'I leaned heavily on my backend teammate' — this deflates your ownership and makes you seem like a passenger.
interview_tips.suggestion: Reframe as: 'I collaborated closely with the backend engineer to design a batching system that aggregated data points, which I then consumed on the frontend to optimize rendering. Together we achieved X result.'

interview_tips.observation: Your CV claims 'architected a scalable microservices backend with Docker and Kubernetes' for CampusEats, but in the interview you only discussed frontend work.
interview_tips.suggestion: Either remove that claim from your CV or prepare to discuss your specific role in the backend architecture. If you didn't build it, say 'I contributed to the frontend of a microservices-based system' — honesty builds trust.

interview_tips.observation: Your answers often start strong but then trail into generalities or defer to teammates.
interview_tips.suggestion: Use the STAR method (Situation, Task, Action, Result) for every answer. End with a clear result or metric to cement your contribution.

interview_tips.observation: You used phrases like 'I'll admit' and 'honestly' when discussing challenges — this can signal insecurity.
interview_tips.suggestion: Replace with confident framing: 'That was a learning curve. I tackled it by...' — own the challenge without apologizing.
